title: Confidence interval for the difference between variants
reading_md:
**What it is.** A confidence interval for the difference between variants is a range of plausible values for the true difference. A 95% interval is built so that, over many repeats of the test, 95% of such intervals contain the true value. If the interval excludes zero, the result is significant at 5%.

**How to work it out.** The unpooled interval:

(p2 - p1) ± 1.96 × sqrt(p1(1 - p1)/n1 + p2(1 - p2)/n2)

Worked example. Control: 500 of 10,000 (p1 = 0.05). Treatment: 560 of 10,000 (p2 = 0.056).

- 0.05 × 0.95 / 10,000 = 0.0000047500
- 0.056 × 0.944 / 10,000 = 0.0000052864
- Sum = 0.0000100364; square root = 0.0031680
- Margin = 1.96 × 0.0031680 = 0.0062093
- Interval = 0.006 ± 0.0062093, so -0.02 to +1.22 percentage points (2 decimals)

The interval includes zero, so the result is not significant at 5%, which matches its p-value of about 0.058. It also shows that a gain of up to 1.22 points is plausible, which a p-value alone hides.

**In the interview.** "Why report an interval rather than only a p-value?" A good answer: it shows both the size of the effect and its uncertainty, so a manager can see the best and the worst plausible case.

**Common mistakes.**

- Reading "there is a 95% chance the true value is in this specific interval" as a strict claim. The 95% describes the method over many repeats.
- Judging significance by whether the two variants' separate intervals overlap. Overlapping intervals can still give a significant difference; build the interval of the difference itself.
- Using the pooled standard error, which belongs to the z-test, for the interval.
